title: Heat Transfer
tagline: Steady and transient conduction, fins, forced and natural convection, boiling and condensation, heat exchangers and thermal radiation
summary: Heat transfer asks how fast thermal energy moves, which sets the size of a radiator, the cooling of a chip and the insulation of a building. The course covers steady and transient conduction, extended surfaces, forced convection in external and internal flows, natural convection, boiling and condensation, heat-exchanger analysis and thermal radiation between surfaces.
overview: Heat transfer is the part of thermodynamics that has to answer a question thermodynamics refuses to: not how much energy is available, but how fast it arrives. A kilowatt of steam and a kilowatt of cooling water are energetically equivalent and engineeringly useless to each other until someone has provided the area, the coefficient and the temperature difference to move the one into the other, and that provision is the whole of this course. Every lesson is built on one rate equation and one resistance network — conduction across a wall, convection across a boundary layer, radiation across a gap of light — and on the observation that the resistances add in series, so that the design problem is almost always to find the largest one and attack it.

The course begins where the physics is easiest and the answers most often taken for granted: one-dimensional steady conduction, in which Fourier's law, a thermal-resistance circuit and a little algebra will size a lagged pipe, a furnace wall or a microprocessor heat-spreader, and will tell you — usually for the first time in a student's career — that a layer of insulation can make a pipe hotter. Fins and two-dimensional shape factors follow, and with them the two ideas that recur everywhere in the subject: that adding surface is a trade between area and the coefficient that drives it, and that a conduction problem you cannot solve can often be read off a table of shape factors computed once and for all by someone who could solve it. Transient conduction then introduces the two dimensionless numbers that govern every heating and cooling operation, Biot and Fourier, the lumped-capacitance method and its failure, the semi-infinite solid that describes a hot ingot dropped on a concrete floor, and the penetration-depth scaling that decides how deep a quench hardens a shaft and how fast a skin burns.

Convection is where the course meets fluid mechanics, and it is honest about the fact that almost everything usable is measured rather than derived. The thermal boundary layer is developed alongside the velocity layer that is its cause, the Reynolds, Prandtl and Nusselt numbers are derived by scaling the energy equation rather than asserted, and the analogy between heat and momentum transfer is used to predict coefficients from friction factors before any correlation is quoted. External flow over plates, cylinders, spheres and tube banks; internal flow in tubes at constant heat flux and constant wall temperature, laminar and turbulent, developing and fully developed; and natural convection, in which buoyancy replaces the pump and the Grashof and Rayleigh numbers replace the Reynolds — three lessons, one method: find the mechanism, find the dimensionless groups, read the correlation, and know its range of validity well enough to know when you are outside it.

The last three lessons are the ones that turn the subject into design. Boiling and condensation supply the largest coefficients in engineering and the most dangerous failure modes, because a surface that crosses the critical heat flux stops being a heat-transfer problem and becomes a metallurgy problem at two thousand degrees; the boiling curve, the Rohsenow and Nusselt analyses and the film-boiling limit are worked until the shape of the curve is memorised, because it is the shape that keeps pressurised water reactors, cryogenic tanks and re-entry vehicles intact. Heat exchangers combine every coefficient in the course into an overall conductance and give the two methods — log-mean temperature difference for sizing, effectiveness–NTU for rating — together with the fouling allowances, correction factors and approach-temperature economics that decide what a plant costs. Radiation, finally, is the only mechanism that needs no material, and it is treated with the machinery it deserves: Planck, Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann, Kirchhoff's law and the selective surfaces it licenses, view factors and the network method, radiation shields, and the band radiation of combustion gases that makes a furnace work and a planet habitable.

The ten lessons are written to be used, not merely read. Every correlation is quoted with its range and its error; every worked example is a machine, a component or an accident rather than a slab of algebra; and every lesson ends with problems in which the answer is a decision — how thick to lag it, how fast to pump it, how far to approach the cold stream, whether to trust the coefficient you have just calculated — because that is the form the question arrives in when you are the one holding the drawing.
outcomes: Set up and solve lumped and distributed thermal-resistance networks for conduction with contact resistances, internal heat generation and critical insulation radii, and state when the one-dimensional assumption fails and by how much

Classify a transient conduction problem by the Biot and Fourier numbers, choose between lumped capacitance, the one-term approximation and the semi-infinite solid, and use penetration-depth scaling to answer hardening, quenching, skin-burn and thermal-cycling questions

Derive the governing dimensionless groups of convection by scaling the energy equation, select the appropriate correlation for external or internal flow with the correct property temperature and characteristic length, and apply the Reynolds–Colburn analogy to obtain heat transfer from friction data

Compute buoyancy-driven flow from the Grashof and Rayleigh numbers, decide whether forced, natural or mixed convection dominates, and size finned and channel-cooled electronics packages using enclosure and optimum-spacing results

Sketch and interpret the pool-boiling curve with its nucleate, transition and film regimes and the critical heat flux, apply the Rohsenow and Nusselt analyses, and explain why a heat exchanger or a reactor core must be designed with margin against the Leidenfrost point

Analyse a heat exchanger by both the log-mean temperature difference method with correction factors and the effectiveness–NTU method, allocate the resistances that control the overall coefficient, apply fouling allowances, and choose an approach temperature from economic rather than optimistic reasoning

Apply Planck's, Wien's and Stefan–Boltzmann's laws with band fractions, use Kirchhoff's law correctly for surfaces exchanging radiation with sources at different temperatures, and solve grey-enclosure problems by the network method including shields and gas radiation

chapters.title: Transient conduction

chapters.summary: Thermal boundary layers, the Nusselt and Prandtl numbers, and heat transfer from plates, cylinders and spheres.

chapters.summary: Developing and fully developed flow in tubes, the mean temperature, and constant heat flux and constant wall temperature.

chapters.title: Natural convection
chapters.summary: Buoyancy-driven flow, the Grashof and Rayleigh numbers, and correlations for plates, cylinders and enclosures.

chapters.title: Boiling and condensation
chapters.summary: Pool boiling and the boiling curve, critical heat flux, flow boiling, and film and dropwise condensation.

chapters.title: Heat exchangers
chapters.summary: Types of heat exchanger, the overall heat-transfer coefficient and fouling, and the LMTD and effectiveness–NTU methods.

history.title: Fourier gives heat a differential equation
history.detail: Joseph Fourier's Théorie analytique de la chaleur, built on a memoir read to the Institut de France in 1807 and published in 1822, states the heat-flux law that carries his name, writes the diffusion equation for a continuous medium, and — decisively for engineering — solves it by superposing sinusoidal modes whose amplitudes are found from the initial condition. Separation of variables and the idea of thermal conductivity as a material property both come from this book, written by a mathematician who had taught at the École Polytechnique, served with Napoleon's expedition to Egypt and then governed the department of Isère as prefect.

history.title: Stokes, and the ancestor of the penetration depth
history.detail: George Gabriel Stokes's 1851 paper on the internal friction of fluids and the motion of pendulums contains the exact solution for a fluid above an oscillating flat plate, showing that a viscous disturbance penetrates a distance proportional to the square root of the kinematic viscosity divided by the frequency. Heat obeys the same square-root law with the thermal diffusivity: Fourier had already treated the periodic heating of the ground, and around 1860 William Thomson (Lord Kelvin) used the solution to reduce J. D. Forbes's Edinburgh underground-temperature records. It is the penetration-depth scaling behind quench, weld and food-freezing estimates.

history.title: Planck quantises the blackbody, and radiation becomes physics
history.detail: Josef Stefan's empirical T-fourth law of 1879 and Boltzmann's 1884 derivation of it leave the spectrum unexplained; Wilhelm Wien's formula of 1896 fits the short wavelengths and fails the long ones, as the measurements of Heinrich Rubens and Ferdinand Kurlbaum showed. In October 1900 Max Planck proposes a formula that fits all the data, and on 14 December 1900 he derives it by assuming that the oscillators of a blackbody exchange energy only in quanta of h nu — the birth of quantum theory, and the reason a heat-transfer course contains constants named after him.

history.title: Prandtl's boundary layer fuses heat and fluid mechanics
history.detail: At the Heidelberg International Congress of Mathematicians Ludwig Prandtl reads a short paper explaining that at high Reynolds number the viscosity matters only in a thin wall layer, so that the flow splits into a nearly inviscid exterior and a diffusive interior. Within two decades his student Heinrich Blasius had solved the laminar flat plate (1908), Theodore von Kármán had given the momentum integral (1921) and Ernst Pohlhausen had solved the thermal layer (1921), while Wilhelm Nusselt's similarity analysis of 1915 supplied the dimensionless groups in which convection coefficients are still correlated.

history.title: Nusselt's film analysis, and boiling becomes a curve
history.detail: In 1916 Wilhelm Nusselt derives the laminar-film condensation coefficient by balancing the drainage of the condensate against conduction across it, obtaining a coefficient that varies as the minus one-quarter power of the temperature difference and of the surface height, with a correction for vertical columns of tubes still used to size condensers. Shiro Nukiyama's 1934 experiments with electrically heated wires in saturated water define the boiling curve and its peak heat flux; T. B. Drew and A. C. Mueller measure the transition region in 1937, and Warren M. Rohsenow's 1952 correlation quantifies nucleate boiling.

history.title: Effectiveness–NTU and compact surfaces
history.detail: The rating question — known area and inlet temperatures, unknown outlets — is awkward with the log-mean temperature difference, and the effectiveness–NTU method answers it directly. A. L. London and R. A. Seban set the method out in a 1942 report that was published only in 1980, and W. M. Kays and A. L. London's Compact Heat Exchangers (1955), built on their Stanford tests of compact surfaces reported as Colburn j-factors and friction factors, made it standard practice.

history.title: Boiling, the critical heat flux and the reactor's limit
history.detail: Post-war reactor programmes, which had to cool fuel with water near or at its boiling point, funded the largest experimental effort in the subject's history. S. S. Kutateladze's dimensional analysis of the critical heat flux (1948–51) and Novak Zuber's hydrodynamic-instability theory of it (1958–59) give the pool-boiling limit, Bergles and Rohsenow's 1964 method predicts the onset of flow boiling, and empirical critical-heat-flux correlations let a reactor designer quote the heat-flux limit with a stated margin.
